_changelog: v1.0.1 (2026-10-16) cold case update reads 5 months later, so the December storm falls inside it
title: Two Heads of Shift
setting: a mountain cable car's two stations

post.author: u/bullwheel_gerolt
post.title: I service a cable car's haul rope at night. At 01:52 my screen showed two PRIMARY banners, and 54 tickets for a cabin with 30 seats.

blocks.text: I'm the night lift mechanic at the bottom station of the Zinnhorn cable car, above Tellach. After the last cabin comes down, I service the haul rope, the moving steel cable that pulls the cabins up the mountain.
The booking system, the program that sells our tickets online, runs on two servers: computers that answer requests day and night. One is in the top station, one down here.

Only one may sell at a time, so no seat goes twice. That one is the primary: ours is the top server. The bottom one is the standby: it keeps a copy of every sale and passes any buyer it gets up to the primary.

They talk through one fibre cable, a glass line buried under the access road. Every second, the top server sends a heartbeat down it, a tiny message that says *I'm still here*. Each station also has its own internet line for buyers; the top one's goes by radio from a roof mast.
If the top server dies, the bottom one takes over by itself. The manual calls that switch failover. We call the primary the head of shift.

It happens in steps. The bottom server listens for heartbeats. After 10 seconds of silence, it holds an election: a vote on who should be primary. It is the only voter, so it votes for itself and wins. Its banner turns to PRIMARY and it starts selling. It phones nobody.

Sunrise seats for the 05:30 cabin go on sale at midnight. Campers and hotel guests in Tellach buy them by phone. The ticket website hands buyers to the two servers in turn: top, bottom, top. Six of the 30 seats were already gone, booked on Friday afternoon by the summit hut.
Tonight, Friday into Saturday, a roadworks crew is digging the access road. They dig only at night, when the road is empty of visitors' cars. At 23:58 their digger cut the fibre.

At 00:20 the foreman knocked to ask whose cable it was. I phoned the fibre company's fault line. Their jointer came at 00:50 and spliced it, joining the glass end to end. At 01:52 my control desk screen beeped: fibre link restored.
Both servers' banners on my screen said PRIMARY.

Then the booking system merged their sales, in steps: it compares the two copies seat by seat, copies a sale only one side has to the other, and lists every seat both sides sold as a conflict. In its report, each line shows the time by that server's own clock, the server (or the merge), its banner and what happened.

00:41:12  top     PRIMARY  seat 12 sold
00:41:37  bottom  PRIMARY  seat 12 sold
01:52:10  merge   24 conflicting seats
54 tickets for 30 seats. Six are the hut's; the other 48 are 24 seats, each sold twice. For 1 hour 54 minutes, I had two heads of shift.

The fibre hadn't failed in six years. We test failover every May: on Tuesday 12 May we switched the top server off, and the bottom one took over in 10 seconds. Nobody ever tested a cut cable with both servers alive.
Each of them was sure the other one was dead.

The bottom server is standby until 23:58:10, primary from 23:58:10 to 01:52:10, then standby again after the merge. Seat 12 is sold by both servers at 00:41. blocks.caption: Green is a server doing its normal job; red is the bottom server acting as primary while the top one is too. The fibre goes quiet at 23:58:00, the bottom server makes itself primary 10 seconds later, and both sell until the splice brings the link back at 01:52:10.

blocks.text: The crew digs all week. Timeline attached. What should we change before the digger comes back?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: There's a name for two servers that both believe they're primary: split brain. Before anyone sells you a fix, look at what each server could actually see. At 23:58:10, did the bottom server know the top one was dead, or only that the fibre was quiet? Did the top server know anything had changed at all? Your May test switched a server off. Tonight both were alive, and only the path between them died. And an election with one voter: what else could it ever decide?

replies.author: u/bullwheel_gerolt
replies.text: No to both. The top server's report shows it selling all night as if nothing had happened. I've phoned our duty manager, who is on call this week: they keep their phone by the bed for night problems. They're driving down to our office in Tellach now. The foreman says the crew digs again tomorrow from 22:00.

comments.author: u/belt_and_braces_edelgard
comments.text: Redundancy, keeping a spare of everything that matters, fixes everything. You had one cable, so one cut parted the stations. Lay a second cable and they can never lose each other again. Your cable car already works this way: two brakes, two motors, two of everything. The network is the one thing nobody doubled.

reply.prompt: The crew digs again tomorrow night. What should the Zinnhorn change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: When the link returns, for each seat sold twice, keep the sale with the later clock time.
options.part2: We set the merge to keep the later clock time. The next night the digger hit the fibre again at 23:58, a metre from the splice. Both servers sold all night. At 01:52 the merge kept the later sale on each of 24 seats and cancelled 24 tickets. Every cancelled ticket came from the top server, and every one had been bought first: each top buyer was 25 seconds ahead of their twin below. 24 people woke to an email saying their sunrise was gone.
options.senior: A merge after the fact can only choose whom to disappoint; the seats were already sold twice. And "later" is only what each server's clock says. Two clocks never agree exactly, so a rule built on them picks winners by accident. That is where Rule 6 begins. Stop the second primary from existing instead.

options.text: Lay a second fibre cable beside the first, so one cut can never part the two stations.
options.part2: The fibre company laid a second cable in the same trench, right beside the first. The next night the digger came back. At 23:58 its bucket went through both. At 01:52 my screen showed two PRIMARY banners again, and the merge reported 24 conflicting seats. Two cables, one trench, one digger.
options.senior: Spares help only when they don't fail together. Two cables in one trench share every cause of failure: a digger, a flood, a landslip. Even a second route only makes a full cut rarer, and the night both go, you have two primaries again. The design has to stay safe while the stations can't talk.

options.text: Add a third voter at the office; only a server holding 2 of 3 votes may sell seats.
options.part2: We put a small computer at the office in Tellach: the witness. It holds no tickets; it only votes. Each server reaches it over its own internet line, not the fibre. The next night the digger cut the fibre again at 23:58. At 23:58:10 the bottom server asked for votes and got only its own: the witness had heard the top server that same second and said no. 1 of 3. It stayed standby. The top server sold all 24 seats, 24 late buyers saw sold out, and at 01:52 the merge found 0 conflicts. One banner said PRIMARY.
options.senior: Let a server be primary only with a majority of votes, 2 of 3, so two can never both win, and put the third voter where a different path reaches it. Give each new primary a higher term number, and make a primary stop selling when its lease runs out without a majority, with the lease shorter than the promotion wait. That is Rule 5: if two claim to be head of shift, neither is.

options.text: Make failover manual: a person on call decides which station's server is the primary.
options.verdict: Trade-off. No split brain, slow at night
options.part2: We turned off automatic failover. Now an alarm phones the duty manager, who decides. The next night the digger cut the fibre again; at 00:46 the manager looked from the office, saw the top server still selling and went back to bed. Nothing sold twice. Two weeks later, at 23:58, lightning killed the top server for real. The alarm rang at 23:58:10, but the manager only made the bottom server primary at 00:46. For 48 minutes nobody could buy a seat: 14 buyers were turned away.
options.senior: A person won't make two primaries in ten seconds, but a person is slow at midnight. You trade split brain for downtime every time the primary really dies at night. It is an honest choice for small systems. A majority vote gives you both: no split brain, and a takeover in seconds.

sim.title: Replay the Zinnhorn's night of two primaries
sim.lede: You're OP at 23:50 on Friday 24 July. The top server is primary; the bottom one is standby and makes itself primary when it has heard nothing from a primary for the promotion wait, 10 s. Seats 1 to 6 are the summit hut's, on both copies. As given, 48 buyers come from midnight in pairs, the first of each pair at :12 past a minute dealt to the top server, the second at :37 to the bottom; pair 6 comes at 00:41. A primary sells its own lowest free seat; a standby passes a buyer up the fibre when it can; otherwise the website tries the other server, and if neither can sell, the buyer is turned away. Pick what fails at 23:58: the fibre (tonight, spliced at 01:52:10), the top server dies, or the whole top station is cut off. Then try a witness (a small third voter at the office that holds no tickets), the majority rule (a server needs 2 of 3 votes to be primary; each election has a term number one higher than the last; and a leader lease: a primary stops selling when no voter has answered it for 5 s, or 30 s), manual failover with the duty manager looking at 00:46, a second fibre in the same trench, or a merge that keeps the later clock time.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play to the end as built. The bottom server is PRIMARY at 23:58:10, seat 12 is sold twice at 00:41:37, and at 01:52:10 two banners say PRIMARY: 54 tickets, 24 seats sold twice, 1 h 54 min with two primaries. Turn on the witness and the majority rule: the bottom server gets 1 of 3 and stays standby, 30 tickets, 0 twice. Now the majority rule without the witness: no split brain, but nobody sells for 1 h 54 min 6 s. Cut off the whole top station with the witness: the bottom wins term 2 with 2 of 3, and a 30 s lease gives 19 s with two primaries. Then try manual failover when the top server dies: 48 min with none.

explain.oneLine: Nothing died. The digger cut the fibre at 23:58, the bottom server heard 10 seconds of silence, held an election with one voter and made itself primary, while the top server, alive and still reached by buyers through its radio mast, kept selling. For 1 hour 54 minutes both sold the same 24 seats.

steps.title: The bottom server mistook a quiet cable for a dead server.
steps.text: In The Copy That Lags (s3e05), a watchdog program made a follower the leader when the leader went quiet: automatic failover. The Zinnhorn's works the same way, in steps. First, the top server sends a heartbeat down the fibre every second. Second, the bottom server counts the silence since the last one. Third, at 10 seconds of silence it holds an election with one voter, itself, and wins. Fourth, it turns its banner to PRIMARY and sells. What goes wrong is the first step's assumption: silence means death. From the bottom station, a dead top server and a cut fibre look exactly the same. The May test only ever tried the first. Tonight's last heartbeat came at 23:57:59, and at 23:58:10 the bottom server was primary, with the top server alive and selling the whole time.

steps.title: Two primaries: split brain.
steps.text: The top server never heard about the bottom server's election, so it never stepped down, and the website still reached it through the radio mast. Each server sold from its own copy, lowest free seat first, so both sold the same seats in the same order: seat 12 went at 00:41:12 on the top and at 00:41:37 below. Two servers each acting as the only primary is called split brain. From 23:58:10 to 01:52:10, 1 hour 54 minutes, each sold seats 7 to 30 to 24 different buyers: 6 hut tickets plus 24 plus 24 makes 54. The merge did its steps correctly, comparing seat by seat, copying one-sided sales and listing 24 conflicts, but a merge can only find the damage, not undo it. Keeping the later clock time would have cancelled the 24 top-server tickets, every one bought 25 seconds before its twin. That is Rule 5: if two claim to be head of shift, neither is, because there is no safe way to choose afterwards. This is not Two Leaders (s3e06), where a commune ran two leaders on purpose and merged their conflicts; here one leader is the design, and two is the failure.

steps.title: An election that needs a majority.
steps.text: The fix is to let a server become primary only when most of the voters agree. In steps: first, a standby that has heard no primary for the wait asks every voter it can reach for its vote in the next term, a numbered round of voting. Second, each voter gives one vote per term, and only if it too has heard no primary for the wait. Third, 2 of 3 votes makes a primary; with three votes in a term, two servers can never both get two. Fourth, the new primary carries the higher term number, and any server that meets a higher term than its own steps down. The third voter here is a witness: a small computer at the office that holds no tickets and only votes, reached by each station's own internet line, a different path from the fibre. Tonight it would have heard the top server that same second and said no: the bottom server gets 1 of 3 and stays standby. What can go wrong: with only the two servers voting, a majority of 2 is 2, so a cut leaves nobody able to win; in the sim nobody sells for 1 h 54 min 6 s. That is why voters come in odd numbers.

steps.title: A lease makes the old primary stop by itself.
steps.text: A majority stops two elections from both succeeding. It does not stop an old primary that never hears about the new one. So the primary holds a lease: it may sell only while a majority has answered it within the last 5 seconds. In steps: each heartbeat that a voter answers renews the lease; if 5 seconds pass with no answer, the primary stops selling and steps down. Because 5 seconds is shorter than the 10 second promotion wait, the old primary has always stopped before anyone else can be elected. In the sim, cut off the whole top station: the top server stops at 23:58:04, the bottom server wins term 2 with 2 of 3 at 23:58:10, and there is never a second primary. With a 30 second lease, both sell for 19 seconds. When the link returns at 01:52:10, the top server sees term 2, higher than its own, and stays standby. The term number does for the primary what s8e01's token did for orders; anything outside the booking system, such as an email, still needs to check it (fencing, s8e02).

steps.title: Why the other fixes fail.
steps.text: A shorter silence before the election only makes the bottom server jump sooner: with 3 seconds it is primary at 23:58:03 and 24 seats still sell twice; with 60 seconds, still 24, because sales open at midnight. A second fibre in the same trench is cut by the same bucket: same 24, same 1 h 54 min. Keeping the later clock time chooses losers after the damage and trusts two clocks that never agree exactly. Manual failover does stop split brain, but a real death at night waits for a person: in the sim, when the top server dies, nobody sells from 23:58:00 until the duty manager acts at 00:46:00, 48 minutes, and 14 buyers are turned away. As built, the same death costs 10 seconds.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn on the night of the cut. The fibre between the top and bottom servers is cut. The top server, primary in term 1, keeps sending heartbeats to the witness at the office, which answers and renews its lease. The bottom server asks the witness for its vote, and the witness refuses because it heard the top server that same second. The bottom server has 1 of 3 votes and stays standby.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn on the night of the cut. The fibre is down, but both servers still reach the witness at the office over their own internet lines. The witness hears the top server every second, so when the bottom server asks for its vote it says no: 1 of 3, and the bottom server stays standby. The top server keeps its lease and sells alone.

fix.title: The fix: a witness, a majority vote, term numbers and a short lease
fix.text: Put a small witness computer at the office in Tellach, reached by each station's own internet line and never by the fibre. Make the bottom server's takeover an election it can lose: it asks for votes in a new term, each voter gives one vote per term and only after hearing no primary for 10 seconds itself, and only 2 of 3 makes a primary. Stamp every new primary with the higher term number, and make any server that meets a higher term step down. Give the primary a 5 second lease that only a majority can renew, so a primary that is cut off stops selling before anyone else can be elected. In the sim, tonight's cut ends with 1 of 3 votes for the bottom server, 30 tickets, 0 seats sold twice and 0 seconds with two primaries.

limits: The witness only helps if it fails separately. Put it in the top station, or on a line that runs through the same trench, and one cut takes away two votes at once; then the station left alone cannot sell at all.

A majority trades some selling for safety. A server that can reach only itself refuses to sell even when it is the only one working, which is correct but costs sales; with only two voters, any cut stops everything, as the sim's 1 h 54 min 6 s with no primary shows.

A lease is measured by each server's own timer. A server that freezes, or whose timer runs slow, can still act on an old lease for a moment; anything that leaves the booking system, such as tickets sent by email, should check the term number too (fencing, s8e02).

explain.seniorTake: A silent link tells you the link is silent, nothing more, so never let one server decide alone that it is now in charge. Make leadership something a server wins from a majority of voters, with an odd number of them, the extra one a small witness on a path that cannot fail together with the others. Number every election with a term, so anything from an older term can be recognised and refused, and give the leader a lease shorter than the wait before a new election, so the old leader has stopped before a new one can start. Then say the cost out loud: a server that cannot reach a majority stops working even if it is healthy, and the witness becomes one more thing to place carefully and watch. Merging after a split is a last resort; by then two people already hold the same seat.

realWorld.title: GitHub, October 2018: 43 seconds and two data centres
realWorld.text: GitHub's post-incident analysis says: "We use Orchestrator to manage our MySQL cluster topologies and handle automated failover." During "routine maintenance work to replace failing 100G optical equipment", the network link was lost "between our US East Coast network hub and our primary US East Coast data center". "Connectivity between these locations was restored in 43 seconds", but in that time "Orchestrator, which had been active in our primary data center, began a process of leadership deselection", and writes moved to the West Coast. Afterwards the database clusters in both data centres "contained writes that were not present in the other data center". Service was degraded for "24 hours and 11 minutes".

realWorld.title: Microsoft: a witness for two-node clusters
realWorld.text: Microsoft's guide to quorum witnesses for Windows Server failover clusters says: "We recommend you always configure a witness if you're using Windows Server 2012 R2 and later." Among the supported cases it lists "Small branch-office clusters, which are even two-node clusters." For a file share witness: "The file share must be dedicated to a single cluster and not used to store user or application data", and "The file share should be physically separate from the cluster nodes or cluster sites."

asked: What is split brain, and how do you prevent it?
Why an odd number of voters?
What does a term number protect against?
interview.answer: Split brain is two copies each acting as the only leader at the same time, usually because the link between them failed and one took silence for death. Both take writes, so the same thing is sold or changed twice, and no merge afterwards can undo it. I prevent it by making leadership a vote, not a timer. A standby that hears nothing asks every voter it can reach for its vote in a new, higher term; each voter gives one vote per term, and only if it has also stopped hearing the leader; a majority makes the new leader. With three voters, two candidates can never both get two votes in one term. With two servers, I'd add a small witness that holds no data and is reached by a different path, so the side that can still reach it wins and the other waits. Voters come in odd numbers because an even split can leave nobody with a majority, and a fourth voter adds no extra failures you can survive over three. The term number protects against an old leader that comes back, or never noticed the election: it carries an older term, so voters and the data refuse it and it steps down. And I'd give the leader a lease shorter than the election wait, so a cut-off leader stops writing before a new one can be elected. The cost is that a side without a majority stops working even if it is healthy. The story I'd tell: a cable car's two booking servers lost their one fibre to a digger at 23:58, the standby promoted itself after 10 seconds while the primary kept selling, and for 1 hour 54 minutes both sold the same 24 seats. GitHub's 2018 outage is the real one: 43 seconds of lost connectivity and two data centres each holding writes the other lacked.

terms.def: The cable car in this story, with a bottom station above the village of Tellach and a top station on the mountain. Its 05:30 sunrise cabin has 30 seats.
The moving steel cable that pulls a cable car's cabins up and down. OP services it at night, after the last cabin.
The program that sells the cable car's seats. It runs on two servers, one in each station, and keeps a record of every sale.
A computer that answers requests from other computers, day and night. The Zinnhorn has one in the top station and one in the bottom station.
The one server allowed to sell, so no seat goes twice. At the Zinnhorn it is the top server. OP's crew calls it the head of shift. Also called the leader.
A server that keeps a copy of every sale and passes buyers up to the primary, ready to take over if the primary dies. Also called a follower.
What OP's crew calls the primary: the one in charge. Rule 5 says there is only one, and if two claim it, neither is.
A cable of thin glass threads that carries messages as light. One runs between the Zinnhorn's stations, under the access road. Also called the link.
A tiny message a server sends on a timer, here every second, to say it is still running. Silence is what makes the other server act.
Switching the job of primary from one server to another when the primary seems to have failed.
Failover done by a program with no person deciding: at the Zinnhorn, the bottom server makes itself primary after 10 seconds of silence (s3e05).
Failover only when a person decides. Option D: the alarm phones the duty manager, who chooses which server is primary.
How long a standby waits without hearing the primary before it tries to become primary. 10 seconds at the Zinnhorn.
A vote among servers on which one should be primary. As built, the Zinnhorn's has one voter, the bottom server, which always votes for itself.
Anything that gets a vote in an election: each server, and in the fix, the witness. Each voter gives at most one vote per term.
More than half of the voters: 2 of 3. Two servers can never both win a majority in the same round of voting.
The number of a round of voting. It goes up by one at each election, so every new primary carries a higher term, and anything from an older term is out of date.
A small third voter that holds no data and only votes, placed where a different path reaches it. In the fix, a computer at the office in Tellach.
Permission to act as primary for a short time, here 5 seconds, renewed only while a majority answers. When it runs out, the primary stops selling.
Two servers each acting as the only primary at the same time, usually after the link between them fails, so both take writes and their copies differ.
How a group of servers chooses one leader, or primary: by a vote that needs a majority, numbered by term.
Combining two copies that changed apart: compare seat by seat, copy what only one side has, and list what both changed as conflicts.
A seat that both servers sold, to different buyers, while they could not talk. Tonight's merge found 24.
A fibre company's technician who splices broken fibre cables, joining the glass end to end so light passes again.
Responsible for answering problems out of hours. The Zinnhorn's duty manager keeps their phone by the bed this week.
The Zinnhorn manager on call this week. OP phoned them at night; in option D, an alarm phones them and they decide which server is primary.
Time when a system cannot do its job. With manual failover, a primary that dies at night means downtime until a person wakes and acts.
Keeping a spare of something important, so one failure does not stop you. It only helps when the spare does not fail at the same time.
A tower that sends and receives radio signals. The top station's internet line goes through one, so it does not use the fibre.
A connection that carries messages between computers or sites, such as the Zinnhorn's fibre, or GitHub's between its East Coast network hub and data centre.
A site where many network lines meet and are passed on. GitHub's East Coast hub joined its main data centre to the rest of its network.
A computer rented by the hour in another company's data centre. A small one makes a good witness because it sits in a third place on its own path.
A building full of computers run together, with power, cooling and network. GitHub had one on each US coast. Also written data center.
A free tool that keeps track of which MySQL copy leads and runs failovers automatically. GitHub used it in 2018.
A widely used free database program. GitHub ran its main databases on it.
Microsoft's name for a group of Windows Server computers that run a service together and fail over between themselves.
Microsoft's name for a witness: a vote held by a disk, a file share or cloud storage, not by a server. A file share is a shared folder on another computer.
There is only one Head of Shift. If two claim to be Head of Shift, neither is. Only a majority can make a primary, so two claimants means a split to stop.
Never trust the clock on the wall. Taught in a later case, Never Trust the Clock; here, the reason a later-clock merge picks losers by accident.
The hands-on project Three regions that must agree, unlocked after s8e01, s8e03, s8e04 and s8e10. This case supplies the majority.
An international standard for running information security. Annex A 8.14 covers redundancy; A 5.30 covers being ready to keep IT running in a disruption.

atWork: Look for any pair of machines that fail over between themselves with no third voter: a primary database and a standby in two buildings, two load balancers that share one address, two schedulers where the spare takes over when the main one goes quiet. A two-node failover pair with no witness is a common pattern, and it works perfectly in every test that switches a machine off. For each one, ask four things. If the link between the two fails while both are alive, which one stops, and how does it know? Who else gets a vote, and does that voter reach each machine by a different path from the link between them? When a machine becomes leader, does it carry a higher number that the data and the other machine check? And does the old leader stop by itself, on a lease shorter than the wait before a takeover? Then test the cut, not just the death: block the link between the two while both run, and count the leaders. On AWS, an RDS Multi-AZ database makes this decision for you; a pair you built yourself on two servers does not. Build Night N6, Three regions that must agree, unlocks after s8e01, s8e03, s8e04 and s8e10; this case supplies its majority. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A 8.14 (redundancy of information processing facilities) and A 5.30 (ICT readiness for business continuity; ICT is short for information and communication technology) expect spare capacity and a tested way to keep running in a disruption. A failover design that has never been tested against a cut link, only a dead machine, would need rework before an audit, so write the cut-link test into the continuity plan from the first draft.

recall.prompt: Your shop's database runs as a pair in two buildings. The standby makes itself primary after 15 seconds without a heartbeat over the one network link between them. A builder cuts that link; both buildings keep taking orders for 40 minutes, and 300 orders clash when it is repaired. A teammate wants a second link and a 5 second wait. What happened, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The old primary was still alive; silence on the link was taken for death, so two primaries took orders at once: split brain
Add a third voter, a witness reached by a different path, and let a server lead only with a majority, 2 of 3
Number each election with a term and give the leader a lease shorter than the wait, so the old primary stops and an older term is refused

recall.model: The old primary wasn't dead; only the link was cut, so the standby took silence for death, made itself primary, and both took orders for 40 minutes: split brain. A second link in the same place can be cut the same way, and a shorter wait only makes the standby jump sooner. I'd add a third voter, a small witness in a third place reached by a different path, and let a server become primary only with a majority, 2 of 3 votes. Each election gets a higher term number, and any server that sees a higher term steps down. The primary also holds a lease shorter than the 15 second wait, renewed only while a majority answers, so a cut-off primary stops taking orders before a new one can be elected.

recall.prompt: Two servers fail over between themselves by voting, and a server needs a majority to lead. Why add a small third voter instead of letting just the two vote?
options: With two voters, winning needs both votes, so when the link between them is cut neither can win and nothing sells
An extra vote makes the counting faster
The extra computer keeps another copy of the tickets in case both servers lose theirs
With only two voters, each server could be chosen in the same round
recall.why: A majority of two is two, so a cut leaves both sides with 1 of 2: no split brain, but no leader either. In the sim, the majority rule without the witness meant nobody sold for 1 h 54 min 6 s. With three voters, the side that still reaches the third wins 2 of 3. The witness holds no data; it only votes.

recall.prompt: Why must a leader's lease be shorter than the wait before another server may hold an election?
options: So the leader saves power while nobody is buying
So a cut-off leader has already stopped acting before a new leader can be elected
So elections happen more often and the best server wins
So the leader's clock and the standby's clock agree
recall.why: A leader that loses its majority doesn't hear about the next election, so it must stop on its own. If its 5 second lease ends before the 10 second wait is over, the old and new leaders never overlap. In the sim, with the top station cut off, a 30 second lease gave 19 seconds with two primaries; a 5 second lease gave none.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: what is split brain, and what protects a system against an old leader that comes back after a new one was chosen?

keyIdeas.idea: Split brain is two copies each acting as leader at the same time, usually after the link between them fails, so both take writes
Leadership needs a majority vote, one vote per voter per round, so only one can win
Each new leader has a higher term number; anything with an older term is refused, and the old leader steps down

recall.model: Split brain is two copies each acting as the leader at the same time, usually because the link between them failed and the standby took silence for death; both accept writes and their data splits. To stop it, a server becomes leader only by winning a majority vote, 2 of 3, where each voter gives one vote per round, so two can't both win; with two servers, add a small witness as the third voter. Each round has a term number, and every new leader carries a higher term. An old leader that comes back carries an older term, so the others and the data refuse its writes and it steps down. A lease shorter than the election wait makes it stop even before it hears.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The witness worked all autumn: the crew cut the fibre twice more, and each time the bottom server got only its own vote and stayed standby. Then the office's internet bill went up, so in November the company moved the witness into a cupboard in the top station. In December a storm brought down the top station's radio mast and the fibre in the same night. The bottom server, the valley line and every ticket machine below were fine, but nothing sold until morning.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did nothing sell, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The witness now sat with the top server, so one failure cut off two of the three votes; the bottom server had only 1 of 3
The bottom server refusing to sell without a majority is the design working: it cannot tell a dead top from a cut-off one
Put the witness back in a third place reached by its own path, so it fails separately from either station

coldCase.model: Moving the witness into the top station put two of the three votes in the same place, so one storm cut off both, and the bottom server could reach only 1 of 3. Refusing to sell without a majority is the design working: from below, it cannot tell a dead top server from a cut-off one, and if it had sold, the top server might have been selling too. The fix is where the witness lives, not the voting. Put it back in a third place, the office or a small cloud machine, reached by its own path from each station, so it never fails together with either one.
